scenes.narration: Picture a thousand passengers at one busy airport. In the old design, they all queue at one checkpoint. Spine leaf gives everyone a short, even path.

scenes.heading: The airport terminal
scenes.narration: Spine leaf has just two tiers. Leaf switches sit at the top of each rack, and connect to the servers. Spine switches form the backbone. Every leaf connects to every spine. So any two servers are always exactly two hops apart.

scenes.heading: Old vs new
scenes.narration: Here's why data centres use it. Paths vary in a three tier network, but spine leaf is always two hops. It suits east west traffic between servers. It uses routing and E C M P instead of spanning tree.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three traps. It's mainly a layer three routed design. Spine switches don't link to each other. And leaf switches don't link to each other either.

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Every leaf connects to every spine. Any two servers are two hops apart. It uses routing and E C M P. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva spine-leaf lab.
